result_expr: Derivative(phi(x, y, z, t), t) - M(T(x, y, z, t))*(6*gamma*eps*(Derivative(phi(x, y, z, t), (x, 2)) + Derivative(phi(x, y, z, t), (y, 2)) + Derivative(phi(x, y, z, t), (z, 2))) - 6*gamma/eps*phi(x, y, z, t)*(1 - phi(x, y, z, t))*(1 - 2*phi(x, y, z, t))) - 30*alpha(T(x, y, z, t))*phi(x, y, z, t)**2*(1 - phi(x, y, z, t))**2*(rho_v(x, y, z, t) - rho_vs(T(x, y, z, t)))

symbols.name: M(T)
symbols.meaning: Interface mobility. It sets how fast $\phi$ relaxes toward a minimum of $F$, and so how fast curvature (Gibbs–Thomson) moves the interface. A positive kinetic coefficient.

symbols.name: alpha(T)
symbols.meaning: Deposition and sublimation rate coefficient: the rate of change of $\phi$ at the interface per unit vapor excess $\rho_v-\rho_{vs}$. It is related to the Hertz–Knudsen kinetic velocity $\beta$ by $\alpha=\beta/(6\varepsilon\rho_i)$.

symbols.name: beta
symbols.meaning: Kinetic velocity of the Hertz–Knudsen law, $\alpha_s\sqrt{k_B T/(2\pi m_w)}$, where $\alpha_s$ is the sticking coefficient. Used only to interpret $\alpha$.

symbols.name: v
symbols.meaning: Normal speed of a planar front

symbols.name: phi0
symbols.meaning: Equilibrium profile of a flat interface

symbols.name: xi
symbols.meaning: Coordinate normal to a flat interface

steps.title: Variational derivative of F
steps.why: The relaxation toward equilibrium is driven by $\delta F/\delta\phi$. We differentiate the double-well density and integrate the gradient term by parts. Boundary terms are dropped (no-flux or periodic boundaries).
steps.operation: Euler–Lagrange variation and integration by parts

check.printed: no tools in this run; checked by hand: d/dphi of phi^2(1-phi)^2 is 2 phi(1-phi)(1-2phi)

steps.title: Check of the flat-interface profile
steps.why: Setting $\delta F/\delta\phi=0$ in 1D gives the flat profile. With this profile $F$ gives energy $\gamma$ and a 10–90 % width of $2\ln 9\,\varepsilon$, so assumption A2 holds for the given $F$.
steps.operation: solve the 1D equilibrium equation and integrate

check.printed: no tools in this run; by hand: the integral of sech^4 over the real line is 4/3, and artanh(0.8)=ln 3

steps.title: Relaxation of the interface
steps.why: $\phi$ is not conserved, because ice mass comes from the vapor. So the simplest dissipative dynamics is linear gradient flow (Allen–Cahn) with a positive mobility $M(T)$.

check.printed: no tools in this run; units by hand: [M][J m^-3] = s^-1

steps.title: Growth and sublimation source
steps.why: Ice deposits when $\rho_v>\rho_{vs}$ and sublimates when $\rho_v<\rho_{vs}$. To first order the source is linear in $\rho_v-\rho_{vs}$. The shape function $30\phi^2(1-\phi)^2$ vanishes in pure gas and pure ice, so there is no nucleation. It integrates to 1 across the interface and does not shift the stable states $\phi=0$ and $\phi=1$.
steps.operation: constitutive choice for the source term

check.printed: no tools in this run; units by hand: m^3 kg^-1 s^-1 times kg m^-3 = s^-1

steps.title: Combined equation
steps.why: Add S3 and S4 and write the Laplacian in Cartesian coordinates. Moving every term to one side gives the residual $R$.
steps.operation: sum of S3 and S4, then substitution of S1

check.printed: no tools in this run; every term has units of s^-1

steps.title: Physical meaning of alpha
steps.why: Put a planar front $\phi_0(\xi-vt)$ into S5, multiply by $\phi_0'$ and integrate over $\xi$. The $F$ terms vanish, and $\int 30\phi_0^2(1-\phi_0)^2\phi_0'\,d\xi=1$. This gives the front speed, which we match to the Hertz–Knudsen law $v=\beta(\rho_v-\rho_{vs})/\rho_i$.

check.printed: no tools in this run; by hand: the S4 source integrates to alpha(rho_v-rho_vs), and the time derivative integrates to -v times 1/(6 eps)

assumptions_used: A1: $\rho_v$ and $T$ are known, smooth fields (given).
A2: The flat interface of $F$ has energy $\gamma$ per unit area and a 10–90 % width of $2\ln 9\,\varepsilon$ (given; checked in S2).
A3: The dynamics of $\phi$ is non-conserved, linear gradient flow with a scalar, isotropic mobility $M(T)>0$.
A4: The deposition rate is linear in the vapor excess $\rho_v-\rho_{vs}(T)$; this is first order in the supersaturation.

A5: Deposition and sublimation act only where ice meets gas. This is imposed with the shape function $30\phi^2(1-\phi)^2$, which vanishes at $\phi=0$ and $\phi=1$ and integrates to 1 across the interface.

neglected.effect: Nonlinear dependence on supersaturation, for example $\ln(\rho_v/\rho_{vs})$
neglected.why: Supersaturations in the pores are small, $|\rho_v/\rho_{vs}-1|\ll1$. The dropped terms are of order $(\rho_v/\rho_{vs}-1)^2$.

neglected.effect: Anisotropy of the ice surface energy and of the attachment kinetics
neglected.why: $\gamma$ is constant by the work order. Faceting at the pore scale is a secondary effect for the bulk transport of ice.
The interface width $\varepsilon\sim\mu$m is much larger than the thermal length $\sqrt{k_BT/\gamma}\sim0.2$ nm.

neglected.effect: Regolith grains as a third phase, including wetting by ice
neglected.why: The work order describes only ice and gas in the pore space. Grains would enter as boundary conditions or as a fixed field.

neglected.effect: Latent heat and vapor mass exchange
neglected.why: They couple $\phi$ back to $T$ and $\rho_v$. Those equations are separate tasks; here the fields are given.

neglected.effect: Elastic stress and mechanical motion of ice
neglected.why: The ice is treated as rigid and fixed in place. Stresses are small compared with the vapor-driven changes.

neglected.effect: A thermodynamically consistent link between $M$ and $\alpha$
neglected.why: I kept them as separate coefficients. Thermodynamic consistency would require $\alpha/M=\rho_i k_BT/(m_w\rho_{vs})$. This changes curvature effects only through the ratio $\varepsilon/$(radius of curvature).

questions: Do you want $M$ and $\alpha$ tied by $\alpha/M=\rho_i k_B T/(m_w\rho_{vs})$? This makes the curvature-driven kinetics consistent with the Gibbs–Thomson effect and the Hertz–Knudsen law. I kept them independent.
Should the driving force be written in the normalized form $(\rho_v-\rho_{vs})/\rho_{vs}$? Then $\alpha$ would be in s$^{-1}$; the physics does not change.
